blocks.text: Application lifespan owns the shared client; requests borrow it. Initialization precedes request handling, and cleanup follows it. Define an @asynccontextmanager async function: acquire before yield, clean up after yield, and register it with FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan). Acquire this application-lifetime resource once rather than repeating startup work in each handler.

blocks.title: Lifespan encloses the request intervals
blocks.alt_text: One application lifetime encloses acquisition, yield, several request intervals borrowing the same client, and cleanup after request handling.

steps.title: Application lifetime is the outer interval

blocks.text: Picture one application lifetime enclosing several requests. Acquire SharedClient before those requests; each handler borrows it without repeating startup work. Cleanup belongs after the request-handling period. Repeating acquisition inside each handler instead describes per-request work, not the one-time startup goal. Choose lifespan for a resource intended to have application lifetime; this does not mean every resource should be global.

In the supplied service, shared_resources holds the client. Acquisition belongs before yield in the async context manager. The yielded interval is the request-handling period; cleanup afterward releases the client when that period finishes. FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan) connects this context to the application. Requests consume the resource, but lifespan owns its startup and cleanup.

Application-lifetime ownership is not per-request acquisition. Sharing this intended application-lifetime client avoids repeated startup work; it is not permission to share every kind of mutable object across requests.
Lifespan initializes before request handling and cleans up afterward.
Acquire before yield, clean up after yield, and register with FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan). Intended application-lifetime resources are acquired once and borrowed by handlers.

blocks.title: Orm relationship mapping
blocks.text: Next: distinguish a stored database association from Python object navigation.

Initialize the intended application-lifetime SharedClient before request handling and clean it up afterward. Handlers borrow that one resource without repeating its startup work. Contrast this with constructing a client in every handler: that is per-request acquisition, not the shared-lifetime goal.

In an @asynccontextmanager async lifespan function, acquisition comes before yield, before the application takes requests. Cleanup comes after yield, after request handling finishes. Register that context with FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan); reversing acquisition and cleanup does not describe this lifetime.

remediation_steps.title: Define the context, then register it

blocks.text: Defining lifespan alone is not registration. Use an @asynccontextmanager async function with client acquisition before yield and cleanup after yield, then pass the function through FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan), rather than leaving the supplied FastAPI() construction unchanged.

An order’s stored customer reference and its Python navigation are separate declarations. Use mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id")) for customer_id and relationship() for related objects or collections. Customer.orders navigates to orders; Order.customer navigates to the customer. Their back_populates values name each other’s relationship attribute, establishing bidirectional in-Python association behavior.

blocks.title: Stored reference versus Python navigation
blocks.alt_text: The stored orders.customer_id reference points to customers.id. Separate Customer.orders and Order.customer navigation arrows name each other through back_populates.

blocks.text: Order.customer_id represents the stored reference to customers.id. Order.customer represents navigation to a Customer object, while Customer.orders is the counterpart collection. On Customer.orders, back_populates="customer" names Order.customer; on Order.customer, back_populates="orders" names Customer.orders. These names identify counterpart attributes, not merely tables. The paired relationships establish bidirectional in-Python association behavior; they do not determine every later loading or query behavior.

blocks.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship
from base import Base

class Customer(Base):
    __tablename__ = "customers"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    orders: Mapped[list["Order"]] = relationship(back_populates="customer")

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    customer_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id"))
    customer: Mapped["Customer"] = relationship(back_populates="orders")

blocks.text: Mapped[list["Order"]] declares collection navigation to Order objects; Mapped["Customer"] declares navigation to one Customer object. These annotations supply the related class to relationship(). Quoting the class name lets Customer refer to Order before Order is declared. The customer_id column separately stores the foreign-key reference. Each back_populates value names the relationship attribute on the opposite class.
A relationship attribute does not replace a database foreign-key column. Stored association and object navigation are declared alongside one another.
Foreign-key columns describe the stored association; relationship() describes object navigation alongside it.
Use mapped_column(ForeignKey(...)) for the reference, and paired back_populates values to name counterpart relationships and establish bidirectional in-Python association behavior.

Order.customer_id is the database reference; relationship() supplies object navigation alongside that reference. Customer.orders and Order.customer pair through back_populates="customer" and back_populates="orders" respectively. Each names the counterpart attribute to establish bidirectional in-Python association behavior—not merely a table name.

Declare customer_id with mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id")) for the stored association. Separately declare related-object or collection navigation with relationship(). Pair Customer.orders and Order.customer by naming each other with back_populates. A navigation attribute does not replace the stored foreign-key column; the paired names establish bidirectional in-Python association behavior.

tiles.title: Declarative field validation constraints / Nested request-data models

blocks.text: An integer type alone does not express an accepted quantity range. Field uses gt/lt for exclusive bounds, ge/le for inclusive bounds, and multiple_of for divisibility. Strings can use min_length, max_length and pattern for length and regular-expression restrictions. Attach Field(...) to the typed model attribute: its constraints apply when constructing the model.

annotations.text: ge/le express the inclusive quantity bounds.
Length bounds constrain this string; no pattern is imposed.
Each probe keeps the other field valid.
With order_reference valid, construction succeeds for quantities 1 and 20; quantities 0 and 21 fail the inclusive range constraint.
With quantity valid, construction succeeds for reference lengths 3 and 12; lengths 2 and 13 fail the length constraints.

blocks.text: The supplied quantity rule runs from 1 through 20, inclusive. Check boundary and neighboring inputs with the other field held valid. ge/le include their boundary; gt/lt exclude it. multiple_of would add a divisibility condition. String length and pattern are different restrictions: meeting one does not prove the other. These are construction-time validation constraints, not just documentation.

For quantity, use Field(ge=1, le=20) on quantity: int to express the inclusive range. If a boundary were excluded, use gt or lt on that side instead. multiple_of adds divisibility without changing the meaning of the bounds. For order_reference: str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=12) expresses the supplied length rule; pattern would express a separate regular-expression restriction. This example imposes no pattern or divisibility requirement. Construction applies the declared constraints.
Do not swap an exclusive bound for an inclusive bound. Work from the rule to the declaration, then inspect the exact boundary values—not just plausible-looking interior values.

An order can compose smaller models for its address and line items. Annotating address: Address incorporates that submodel’s validation; line_items: list[LineItem] validates the corresponding collection data. Nested validation errors can locate a failed field using enclosing field names and element indexes. Follow the location inward rather than looking only at the order’s outer fields.

annotations.text: Input path: line_items → index 1 → quantity. This is the second item’s invalid quantity, not an outer field.
The address field validates the address input with Address.
The collection validates its input objects with LineItem.
Follow line_items to the second item and then quantity in this input. Error locations can include field names and indexes.

blocks.text: Address declares street; LineItem declares product and quantity. Order composes one Address and a list of LineItem models. In the supplied invalid input, the second item’s quantity is a nonnumeric string. Follow a nested location through line_items, the element index, then quantity to identify that part of the input. Outer-field and nested-field failures both belong to enclosing-model validation, but their locations identify different input parts.
An enclosing Order does not make an invalid nested value acceptable. Each submodel’s validation participates in validation of the enclosing model.
Field constraints on typed attributes apply during construction. Distinguish inclusive/exclusive bounds, divisibility, string length and pattern.
Submodel and list-of-submodel annotations compose nested validation. Error locations identify failed fields using names and collection indexes.

The supplied quantity rule includes its endpoints: Field(ge=1, le=20). ge/le include the boundary, whereas gt/lt exclude it. multiple_of adds divisibility as another numeric restriction rather than changing which bound is inclusive. Compare the rule’s exact endpoint with an interior value before choosing a bound.

remediation_steps.title: Length rule on the typed attribute

blocks.text: For order_reference: str, attach Field(min_length=3, max_length=12) to the attribute so model construction applies the length constraints. pattern would add a regular-expression restriction; length alone is not proof of a pattern match. The supplied example has a length rule only. A typed attribute without this Field declaration does not express that rule.

Order.address incorporates Address validation, and Order.line_items incorporates LineItem validation. Enclosing the data in Order does not make a bad nested value acceptable. For the supplied nonnumeric quantity, follow the collection name to the second item and then the quantity field; a nested location can include both names and indexes.

address: Address validates one nested object; line_items: list[LineItem] validates corresponding collection data. In the supplied invalid input, follow line_items to the second element and its quantity field, not to the address. Nested error locations can use collection element indexes as well as field names.
